\title{\textbf{\Large Pre-Planned Response Surface Methodology and Face-Centered Central Composite Design for Multi-Objective Hyperparameter Optimization in Gradient Boosted Trees under Stochastic Nuisance Blocking}}

\author{
    \textbf{Christos Chousein Sounios}
}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Hyperparameter optimization in gradient boosted decision trees is commonly conducted using adaptive black-box search methods, which offer strong point optimization performance but limited parametric attribution of factor effects and data-split nuisance variation. We evaluate a classical Design of Experiments (DOE) and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) framework based on Douglas C. Montgomery's methodology to study and optimize an XGBoost regressor across four hyperparameters on the California Housing dataset ($N = 20{,}640$) under stochastic nuisance blocking. A pre-planned, globally randomized 140-run Face-Centered Central Composite Design (FCCD) across five deterministic seed blocks isolates data-partition variance ($\sigma_{\text{block}} \approx \numSigmaBlock$ RMSE, $\text{ICC} = \numICCAnova$ of unexplained residual variance) and is analyzed in two hierarchical stages: factorial-plus-center screening ($N_1 = 100$) and full second-order augmentation ($N_{\text{CCD}} = 140$, where $\numDoeAxialBeforeHundred$ of $40$ axial runs occur at $\texttt{run\_order} \le 100$). Screening detects strong response curvature ($\bar{y}_F - \bar{y}_C = +\numDiffCurv$ RMSE, $+\numCurvPctIncrease$; $F = \numFCurv$ against within-block center subsampling error, $F = \numCurvFBlockAdjPooled$ against $79$-df block-adjusted pooled error, and $F = \numCurvFBlockPaired$ across $5$ paired blocks), while second-order lack-of-fit decomposition ($F = \numFLofYone$) shows that quadratic polynomial surrogates serve as local guidance maps rather than globally exact estimators of boosting loss. Canonical analysis reveals a stationary/rising ridge system, and Derringer-Suich desirability optimization identifies a compromise coordinate ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$, depth 4) confirmed across $m = 10$ fresh seeds, whereas the single-objective boundary candidate ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$, depth 7) exhibits $+\numConfSoBias$ RMSE polynomial optimism bias. In a prospective 20-replicate benchmark campaign ($\numRevTotalFits$ model fits, $\numRevTotalTimedInferences$ timed inferences; \numRevTotalSelectionRecords\ frozen selection records across \numRevTotalDistinctConfigs\ distinct configurations evaluated on $20$ fresh seeds on the $4{,}128$-row holdout test set), Single-Objective TPE achieves the lowest observed test RMSE ($\numRevSoTpeTestRMSE \pm \numRevSoTpeTestRMSESd$) by concentrating all $140$ adaptive trials in deeper trees ($d \in \{7, 8, 9\}$) at higher latency ($\numRevSoTpePredictLat \pm \numRevSoTpePredictLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$), whereas Repeated DOE Single-Objective yields deterministic boundary selection ($\numRevDoeSoTestRMSE$, conditional retraining $\sigma_{\text{eval}} = \numRevDoeSoRetrainSd$) with \numRevDoeSoLatLowerPct\ lower latency ($\numRevDoeSoPredictLat \pm \numRevDoeSoPredictLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$). In latency-constrained multi-objective optimization ($\le 145\,\mu\text{s}$), Repeated DOE and Multi-Objective TPE show no statistically significant difference in holdout test RMSE ($\numRevDoeMoTestRMSE$ vs.\ $\numRevMoTpeTestRMSE$, primary Welch $p = \numRevWelchPDoeMoMoTpe$) at comparable latency ($\numRevDoeMoPredictLatOneDp$ vs.\ $\numRevMoTpePredictLatOneDp\,\mu\text{s}$) and $100\%$ ($20/20$) feasibility, while contributing jointly to a \numRevHoldoutNonDominatedConfigs-point holdout non-dominated frontier (seed-bootstrap $\text{HV} = \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedMean \pm \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedSd$).
\end{abstract}

\vspace{0.5em}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Design of Experiments (DOE), Response Surface Methodology (RSM), Central Composite Design (CCD), Gradient Boosted Trees, XGBoost, Multi-Objective Optimization, Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD), Canonical Analysis, Model Adequacy.

\section{Introduction and Theoretical Framework}

Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs), such as XGBoost \cite{chen2016xgboost}, achieve competitive predictive accuracy on tabular data. However, tuning GBDT hyperparameters involves non-linear interactions, non-convex loss surfaces, and operational trade-offs between predictive accuracy and single-sample inference latency.

Standard practice relies on heuristic and adaptive search algorithms, including uniform random search \cite{bergstra2012random} and Bayesian optimization methods such as Tree-structured Parzen Estimators (TPE) \cite{bergstra2011algorithms, akiba2019optuna} or Gaussian Process regression. In practical workflows, these black-box optimizers present three structural trade-offs relative to parametric response surface methods:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item \textbf{Absence of Parametric Attribution:} Black-box optimizers treat the objective function as an opaque evaluation oracle. They do not decompose variance across main effects, two-factor interactions, and quadratic terms, nor do they provide a closed-form polynomial surrogate for canonical sensitivity analysis.
    \item \textbf{Confounding of Stochastic Nuisance:} Variation arising from random data partitioning and stochastic subsampling is confounded with hyperparameter sensitivity unless structured blocking or repeated multi-split evaluation is introduced.
    \item \textbf{Lack of Curvature and Adequacy Tests:} Heuristic search strategies do not provide formal ANOVA hypothesis tests to determine whether an operational region is planar, locally quadratic, or structurally misfitted by low-order polynomials.
\end{enumerate}

To evaluate these trade-offs against adaptive search under matched evaluation budgets, this study implements a pre-planned, two-stage hierarchical Design of Experiments (DOE) and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) pipeline based on Chapters 4, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, and 13 of Douglas C. Montgomery's \textit{Design and Analysis of Experiments} \cite{montgomery2017design}, following response surface methodology developed by Box and Wilson \cite{box1951experimental} and extended by Myers et al.\ \cite{myers2016response}. By combining randomized complete block screening, multi-denominator curvature testing, Face-Centered Central Composite Design (FCCD) modeling, spectral canonical analysis, and Derringer-Suich desirability functions \cite{derringer1980simultaneous}, we examine both the variance-attribution strengths and the boundary-allocation and polynomial-misfit limitations of classical RSM on GBDT hyperparameter surfaces.

All metrics, sums of squares, test statistics, and diagnostics reported in this paper are derived from model fits on the California Housing benchmark ($N = 20,640$). An external holdout test set of 4,128 observations (20\%) was set aside from the 16,512-observation development pool, which each seed block partitioned into 12,384 training (75\%) and 4,128 validation (25\%) samples. Whereas the historical $v1.0.0$ experiments recorded test results during development, the revised pipeline prevented access to those test labels during all surrogate fitting, curvature testing, lack-of-fit analysis, and desirability optimization until winning configurations were frozen in \texttt{finalized\_selections.json}. These safeguards enforce programmatic holdout isolation during the revised search, although they cannot retroactively undo earlier exposure of the same dataset.

\section{Experimental Architecture and Mathematical Formulation}

\subsection{Operational Factors and Standard Coding}

We define four hyperparameter factors (three continuous, one integer depth) controlling structural complexity and regularization for an XGBoost regressor with $n_{\text{estimators}} = 100$:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.8em]
    \item \textbf{Factor A ($x_1$):} Learning rate ($\eta \in [0.01, 0.30]$), coded on a logarithmic scale: $\xi_1 = \ln(\eta) \in [\ln(0.01), \ln(0.30)] = [-4.6052, -1.2040]$.
    \item \textbf{Factor B ($x_2$):} Maximum tree depth ($\text{depth} \in [3, 9]$), controlling structural model complexity.
    \item \textbf{Factor C ($x_3$):} Subsample fraction ($\text{subsample} \in [0.50, 1.00]$), introducing stochastic row subsampling.
    \item \textbf{Factor D ($x_4$):} $L_2$ leaf regularization ($\lambda \in [0.10, 10.00]$), coded on a logarithmic scale: $\xi_4 = \ln(\lambda) \in [\ln(0.10), \ln(10.00)] = [-2.3026, 2.3026]$.
\end{itemize}

Each natural variable $\xi_i$ is mapped to dimensionless coded space $x_i \in [-1, +1]$ via:
\begin{equation}
    x_i = \frac{\xi_i - \frac{\xi_{i,\max} + \xi_{i,\min}}{2}}{\frac{\xi_{i,\max} - \xi_{i,\min}}{2}}, \quad i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}
\end{equation}
The operational domain forms a 4-dimensional hypercube $\mathcal{D} = [-1, +1]^4$. Table \ref{tab:factor_levels} summarizes factor coding.

\subsection{Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD), Study Chronology, and Budget Allocation}

Stochastic variation in data partitioning and subsampling introduces non-trivial variance across evaluation trials. We structure the experimental protocol as a Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD) across $b = 5$ distinct seed blocks: $\mathcal{S} = \{42, 101, 202, 303, 404\}$. Table \ref{tab:design_block_seeds} summarizes the assignment of split seeds and model seeds across phases.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.25}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3.5pt}
\input{tables/tab_design_block_seeds.tex}
\vspace{0.6em}
\caption{Structure of Blocks, Split Seeds, and Model Seeds Across Experimental Phases}
\label{tab:design_block_seeds}
\end{table}

Specifically, each block $b$ defines a distinct 75/25 train/validation partition of the 16,512 development observations via split seed $S_b$. For corner runs ($1 \dots 16$) and axial runs ($18 \dots 25$), the internal XGBoost subsampling seed is also set to $S_b$, meaning that the block factor captures the joint nuisance impact of data-split selection and stochastic subsampling realization. For the four center point replicates within block $b$, the train/validation split is held fixed at $S_b$ while the model subsampling seed is varied via $S_b + r \times 1000$ ($r \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$), isolating within-block stochastic subsampling pure error ($15$ degrees of freedom) from block-to-block variation ($4$ degrees of freedom).

\textbf{Actual Study Chronology vs.\ Two-Stage Hierarchical Analysis:} In the execution script (\texttt{pipeline.py}), all $28 \times 5 = 140$ runs of the Face-Centered Central Composite Design ($16$ factorial corners, $4$ center replicates, and $8$ axial points per block) were generated upfront and globally randomized into a single execution schedule ($\texttt{run\_order} \in \{1, \dots, 140\}$). In this randomized schedule, exactly $\numDoeAxialBeforeHundred$ of the $40$ \texttt{Phase2\_Axial} runs were executed at $\texttt{run\_order} \le 100$, interleaved with \texttt{Phase1\_Factorial} runs. Thus, Phase~1 ($N_1 = 100$) and Phase~2 ($N_{\text{CCD}} = 140$) denote a two-stage hierarchical statistical decomposition of a pre-planned 140-run FCCD rather than an adaptive sequential design in which axial runs were conditioned on observing Phase~1 outcomes.

\textbf{Budget Allocation Trade-Off ($25$ Replicated Coordinates vs.\ $140$ Distinct Configurations):} Under the matched 140-evaluation budget per search campaign, the blocked FCCD evaluates $25$ distinct hyperparameter coordinates replicated across $5$ seed blocks ($125$ coordinate-block evaluations plus $15$ extra center runs $= 140$ fits). Because a $2^4$ factorial plus face-centered axial design places $8$ corners and $1$ axial point per block at the lower learning-rate boundary $x_1 = -1.0$ ($\eta = 0.01$), exactly $\numDoeLowEtaCount/140$ runs ($\numDoeLowEtaPct$) evaluate $\eta = 0.01$, where 100-tree ensembles underfit (mean validation RMSE $\numDoeLowEtaMeanRMSE$ vs.\ $\numDoeHighEtaMeanRMSE$ for $x_1 > -1.0$). By contrast, adaptive TPE and Random Search allocate all $140$ evaluations to distinct hyperparameter configurations on a single validation split without cross-block replication, trading variance-component identifiability and multi-split blocking for denser interior coordinate exploration.

The statistical model for response $y_{uj}$ at design point $u$ in block $j$ is:
\begin{equation}
    y_{uj} = \mu + \tau_u + \beta_j + \epsilon_{uj}, \quad j \in \{1, \dots, 5\}
\end{equation}
where $\tau_u$ represents the treatment effect of design coordinate $\mathbf{x}_u$, $\beta_j$ represents the block effect, and $\epsilon_{uj}$ is experimental error.

To quantify the magnitude of variance absorbed by blocking, we compute the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) under both ANOVA and REML formulations:
\begin{equation}
    \text{ICC} = \frac{\sigma^2_{\text{block}}}{\sigma^2_{\text{block}} + \sigma^2_\epsilon}
\end{equation}
For validation RMSE, the ANOVA estimator yields $\text{ICC} = \numICCAnova$ ($F = \numFBlock, p \numPBlock$), which matches the restricted maximum likelihood estimate ($\text{ICC}_{\text{REML}} = \numICCReml$). Importantly, this \numICCAnovaPct\ represents a share of \textit{unexplained residual variance} rather than total experimental variation (where primary factors account for $>90\%$ of total sum of squares). In absolute terms, the estimated block standard deviation is $\sigma_{\text{block}} = \sqrt{\sigma^2_{\text{block}}} \approx \numSigmaBlock$ RMSE. This nuisance variation is comparable in magnitude to the performance differences separating competitive hyperparameter configurations (often $0.005$--$0.015$ RMSE), which makes blocking necessary when comparing close configurations.

While the block effect is non-significant in Phase~1 ($F = \numAnovaPOneFBlock, p = \numAnovaPOnePBlock$), it is significant in the Phase~2 second-order model ($F = \numFBlock, p < 10^{-11}$). This difference reflects variance shielding: in Phase~1, unmodeled quadratic curvature pooled into the residual denominator ($\text{MS}_E = \numAnovaPOneMSE$), inflating error variance and attenuating the block $F$-ratio. Once second-order terms accounted for curvature in Phase~2 ($\text{MS}_E$ reduced to $\numAnovaCCDMSE$), seed partition variance became detectable. For inference latency, the block effect is negligible ($\text{ICC} = \numICCLatency, F = \numFBlockLatency, p = \numPBlockLatency$), as execution speed is governed by hardware architecture and tree topology rather than data splits.

\subsection{Dual Responses and Latency Measurement Protocols}

For every trial, two responses are measured:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Response $Y_1$ (Development Validation RMSE):} Root mean squared error evaluated on the 25\% validation partition ($N_{\text{val}} = 4,128$) of the development pool. Unlike the historical $v1.0.0$ pipeline, which recorded test metrics during development, the revised pipeline prevented access to the holdout 20\% test partition ($N_{\text{test}} = 4,128$) until candidate configurations were frozen for final generalization testing.
    \item \textbf{Response $Y_2$ (Single-Sample Inference Latency):} Execution time in microseconds per single sample ($\mu\text{s/sample}$) on CPU. We emphasize that this represents single-sample point evaluation rather than batched throughput, and the quadratic depth term is an empirical response-surface fit across sampled depths $d \in \{3, 6, 9\}$.
\end{enumerate}

Latency measurements across the study follow three explicitly distinguished protocol tiers:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item \textbf{Pinned CPU Affinity and Single-Threaded Execution:} Across all historical and prospective scripts, the execution process is pinned to CPU Core 0 via Windows API \texttt{SetProcessAffinityMask(\allowbreak GetCurrentProcess(), 1)} with single-threaded XGBoost inference (\texttt{n\_jobs=1}) timed via \texttt{time.\allowbreak perf\_counter\_ns}.
    \item \textbf{Historical DOE, Confirmation, and Baseline Protocol (\texttt{results/runs.csv}, \texttt{confirmation\_\allowbreak runs*.csv}, \texttt{benchmark.csv}):} Each model fit executes 100 untimed warmup calls (50 per prediction interface) followed by 1,000 timed single-sample calls per interface.
    \item \textbf{Prospective Online Search vs.\ Holdout Verification Protocols (\texttt{full\_run\_001}):} During prospective search (\texttt{optimizer\_trials.csv} and \texttt{doe\_selection\_\allowbreak runs.csv}), candidate models are timed using 30 un-warmed single-row \texttt{predict} calls per fit (\texttt{online\_30call\_\allowbreak single\_row\_cpu0}) to bound wall-clock cost across $14{,}000$ search fits. During final holdout verification (\texttt{final\_evaluations.csv}), each frozen configuration is timed across 2 independent sessions of 25 warmup calls per interface (50 total) and 500 timed single-row calls per interface per session ($1{,}000$ timed calls/seed; between-session $\text{SD} = \numRevBetweenSessionSd\,\mu\text{s}$).
    \item \textbf{Interface Overhead (\texttt{Booster.predict(DMatrix)} vs.\ \texttt{XGBRegressor.\allowbreak inplace\_predict}):} Standard \texttt{predict} constructs a \texttt{DMatrix} wrapper and validates 2D array metadata on each single-row call, whereas \texttt{inplace\_predict} operates directly on the 2D NumPy buffer. The measured per-sample overhead of \texttt{predict} minus \texttt{inplace\_predict} is $\numHistRunsOvMean \pm \numHistRunsOvSd\,\mu\text{s}$ (range $\numHistRunsOvMin$--$\numHistRunsOvMax\,\mu\text{s}$) across the 140 historical DOE runs, $\numHistConfMoOvMean \pm \numHistConfMoOvSd\,\mu\text{s}$ ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$) and $\numHistConfSoOvMean \pm \numHistConfSoOvSd\,\mu\text{s}$ ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$) in historical confirmation, $\numHistBenchOvMean \pm \numHistBenchOvSd\,\mu\text{s}$ (range $\numHistBenchOvMin$--$\numHistBenchOvMax\,\mu\text{s}$) in the historical benchmark, and $\numRevInterfaceOverhead \pm \numRevInterfaceOverheadSd\,\mu\text{s}$ (range $\numRevInterfaceOverheadMin$--$\numRevInterfaceOverheadMax\,\mu\text{s}$) in the 50-configuration Revision-v2 interface audit (\texttt{latency\_interface\_\allowbreak overhead.json}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Phase 1: Factorial Screening and Curvature Assessment}

Phase~1 analyzes the $2^4$ full factorial subset consisting of $n_F = 16$ corner runs, augmented with $n_C = 4$ center points per block ($x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = x_4 = 0$). Evaluated across all 5 seed blocks, this screening stage comprises $N_1 = 100$ model training runs.

We fit a first-order response surface model with all two-factor interaction terms:
\begin{equation}
    Y = \beta_0 + \sum_{i=1}^4 \beta_i x_i + \sum_{i < j} \beta_{ij} x_i x_j + \sum_{b=2}^5 \gamma_b Z_b + \epsilon
\end{equation}
where $Z_b$ are dummy indicators for blocks $2$ through $5$. Table \ref{tab:anova_phase1} details the Type III Sum of Squares ANOVA for Response $Y_1$.

\centering

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{5.5pt}

\vspace{0.6em}
\caption{Phase 1 ANOVA Table (Type III Sum of Squares) for Validation RMSE ($Y_1$)}
\label{tab:anova_phase1}
\end{table}

Factor A ($\ln(\eta)$) dominates predictive performance ($F = \numAnovaPOneFxone, \text{partial } \eta^2 = \numAnovaPOneEtxone$), followed by Factor B (tree depth, $F = \numAnovaPOneFxtwo$) and the interaction $x_1 \cdot x_2$ ($F = \numAnovaPOneFxoneXtwo, p < 10^{-6}$).

\subsection{Formal Curvature Hypothesis Test and Error-Denominator Sensitivity}

Following Montgomery (Chapter 11), overall quadratic curvature $H_0: \sum_{i=1}^4 \beta_{ii} = 0$ is tested via the single-degree-of-freedom contrast between the factorial corner mean ($\bar{y}_F$) and the center-point mean ($\bar{y}_C$):
\begin{equation}
    \text{SS}_{\text{Curvature}} = \frac{n_F n_C (\bar{y}_F - \bar{y}_C)^2}{n_F + n_C}
\end{equation}
Across the 100 runs evaluated in Phase~1:
\begin{equation}
    n_F = 80, \quad \bar{y}_F = \numMeanFactorial, \quad n_C = 20, \quad \bar{y}_C = \numMeanCenter, \quad \bar{y}_F - \bar{y}_C = +\numDiffCurv \ (+\numCurvPctIncrease)
\end{equation}
yielding $\text{SS}_{\text{Curvature}} = \numSSCurv$. When tested against within-block center-point pure error ($\text{df} = \numDFpeCenter, \text{MS}_{\text{PE, Center}} = \numMSpeCenter$), the resulting $F$-ratio is:
\begin{equation}
    F_{\text{Curvature}} = \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{Curvature}}}{\text{MS}_{\text{PE, Center}}} = \numFCurv \quad (p < 10^{-15})
\end{equation}
Why is $F_{\text{Curvature}} = \numFCurv$ of order $10^5$? Two structural features of the design explain this magnitude: (i) the numerator ($\text{SS}_{\text{Curvature}} = \numSSCurv$) captures a macro-scale hyperparameter contrast across the full cube where half of all corner runs lie at $\eta = 0.01$ and severely underfit ($\bar{y}_F = \numMeanFactorial$ vs.\ $\bar{y}_C = \numMeanCenter$), and (ii) the denominator ($\text{MS}_{\text{PE, Center}} = \numMSpeCenter$, $\text{SD} = \numSqrtMSPeCenterYone$ RMSE) isolates micro-scale stochastic row-subsampling variability ($s = 0.75$) on a \textit{fixed} train/validation partition $S_b$, excluding split-by-treatment interaction and higher-order factorial terms.

To ensure that curvature inference does not rely on this narrow subsampling denominator, we evaluate $\text{SS}_{\text{Curvature}} = \numSSCurv$ across six broader error specifications:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), itemsep=0.2em]
    \item \textbf{Block-Adjusted Pooled Coordinate Error ($\text{df} = 79$):} Pooling within-block center pure error ($15$~df) with the Phase~1 Treatment $\times$ Block interaction ($64$~df) yields $\text{MS} = \numCurvMSBlockAdjPooled$ and $F = \numCurvFBlockAdjPooled$ ($p < 10^{-15}$).
    \item \textbf{Phase~1 Treatment $\times$ Block Interaction ($\text{df} = 64$):} Testing directly against coordinate-by-split interaction across the $17 \times 5$ cells ($\text{MS} = \numCurvMSTxB$) yields $F = \numCurvFTxB$ ($p < 10^{-15}$).
    \item \textbf{Block-Paired Contrast Across the 5 Seed Blocks ($\text{df} = 4$):} Computing $d_b = \bar{y}_{F,b} - \bar{y}_{C,b}$ within each block $b \in \{1, \dots, 5\}$ treats the block as the independent experimental unit, yielding $\bar{d} = +\numDiffCurv$ RMSE ($\text{SE} = \numCurvSEBlockPaired$, 95\% CI $[\numCurvCIBlockPairedLow, \numCurvCIBlockPairedHigh]$), paired $t = \numCurvTBlockPaired$, and $F = t^2 = \numCurvFBlockPaired$ ($p = \numCurvPBlockPaired$).
    \item \textbf{Unadjusted Coordinate Pure Error ($\text{df} = \numDFpeAll$):} Pooling within-coordinate variance across all 17 Phase~1 coordinates without removing block main effects ($\text{MS}_{\text{PE, All}} = \numMSpeAll$) yields $F = \numCurvFPeCoordUnadj \approx \numFCurvAll$ ($p < 10^{-15}$).
    \item \textbf{First-Order + 2FI + Curvature Residual ($\text{df} = 84$):} Testing against the residual of the 16-parameter block + main + 2FI + curvature model ($\text{MS} = \numCurvMSTwoFICurvResid$, which pools $3$FI+$4$FI interactions, Treatment $\times$ Block, and center pure error) yields $F = \numCurvFTwoFICurvResid$ ($p < 10^{-15}$).
    \item \textbf{Unadjusted First-Order + 2FI Residual ($\text{df} = 85$):} Even against the unadjusted Phase~1 residual mean square before separating curvature ($\text{MS}_E = \numCurvMSTwoFIResid$), the ratio is $F = \numCurvFTwoFIResid$ ($p = \numCurvPTwoFIResid$).
\end{enumerate}
Under every error specification, planarity is rejected by a wide margin. Crucially, rejecting $H_0: \sum \beta_{ii} = 0$ establishes the \textit{presence of strong non-planarity} across $[-1, +1]^4$; it does not establish that a second-order polynomial is an adequate global functional form. Surrogate predictive adequacy is tested separately via Phase~2 lack-of-fit decomposition (Section~\ref{sec:lof}) and Phase~5 confirmation trials (Section~\ref{sec:confirmation}).

\section{Phase 2: Second-Order Response Surface Modeling and Adequacy}

\subsection{Face-Centered Central Composite Design (FCCD)}

Incorporating the $2k = 8$ face-centered axial coordinates ($\alpha = 1.0$) across the 5 seed blocks ($40$ axial runs, cumulative $N_{\text{CCD}} = 140$ runs across $25$ distinct coordinates) enables estimation of the full second-order polynomial response surface:
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
    Y = \beta_0 &+ \sum_{i=1}^4 \beta_i x_i + \sum_{i=1}^4 \beta_{ii} x_i^2 \\
    &+ \sum_{i < j} \beta_{ij} x_i x_j + \sum_{b=2}^5 \gamma_b Z_b + \epsilon
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Table \ref{tab:anova_ccd_rmse} reports the second-order ANOVA for Validation RMSE ($R^2 = \numRsqRMSE, \text{Adj } R^2 = \numAdjRsqRMSE$). Because residual variance varies across the factor domain, both OLS and HC3 hetero\-scedasticity-consistent standard errors and p-values are reported.

Under HC3 covariance estimation, structural effects $x_1, x_2, x_1^2, x_2^2, x_1 x_2$, and $x_1 x_4$ remain significant ($p < 0.0001$). \subsection{Lack-of-Fit Decomposition and Structural Model Adequacy}
\label{sec:lof}

In response surface methodology \cite{montgomery2017design}, evaluating model adequacy requires decomposing the model residual sum of squares into pure experimental error and structural lack of fit. In our blocked central composite design ($N=140$ runs across 5 blocks), non-center design coordinates are observed once per block. Genuine within-coordinate and within-block replication exists exclusively at the center points ($x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = x_4 = 0$), where 4 model-seed replicates within each of the 5 blocks provide exactly $\text{df}_{\text{PE, center}} = 5 \times (4 - 1) = 15$ degrees of freedom of genuine within-cell pure replicate error ($\text{SS}_{\text{PE, center}} = \numSSPeCenterYone$, $\text{MS}_{\text{PE, center}} = \numMSPeCenterYone$).

Fitting a saturated additive cell model containing all $m=25$ unique design coordinates and 4 block parameters (29 parameters) leaves $140 - 29 = 111$~degrees of freedom with $\text{SS} = \numSSPeYone$ ($\text{MS} = \numMSPeYone$). Rather than representing uniform replicate noise, these $111$~df decompose into:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item Genuine center-point pure replicate error ($15$~df, $\text{SS} = \numSSPeCenterYone$);
    \item Treatment $\times$ Block interaction / split-specific treatment response ($111 - 15 = 96$~df, $\text{SS} = \numSSInteractYone, \text{MS} = \numMSInteractYone$).
\end{enumerate}
Evaluating the interaction against center pure error yields $F = \numFInteractCenterYone$ ($p = \numPInteractCenterYone$), establishing statistically significant split-by-hyperparameter interaction: different train/validation data splits exhibit subtle variations in optimal response curvature.

The remaining $121 - 111 = 10$~df represent structural lack of fit ($\text{SS}_{\text{LoF}} = \numSSLofYone, \text{MS}_{\text{LoF}} = \numMSLofYone$). Table \ref{tab:lof} details this complete decomposition for both responses.

\centering

\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\input{tables/tab_lof.tex}
\vspace{0.6em}
\caption{Residual Variance Decomposition (121 df), Lack-of-Fit Tests, and Domain Restriction Sensitivity}
\label{tab:lof}
\end{table}

For Validation RMSE ($Y_1$) on the full operational domain:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item Tested against center pure error ($15$~df), lack of fit is statistically significant ($F = \numFLofCenterYone, p < 10^{-15}$).
    \item Tested against the saturated additive baseline ($111$~df, pooling interaction and replicate noise), lack of fit is also significant ($F = \numFLofYone, p = \numPLofYone$).
\end{itemize}
Under either reference baseline, the root-mean-square misfit per degree of freedom is $\sqrt{\text{MS}_{\text{LoF}}} = \numSqrtMSLofYone$, which is approximately $\numLofRatioAdditive\times$ the additive residual standard deviation ($\sqrt{\text{MS}_{\text{PE}}} = \numSqrtMSPeYone$) and $\numLofRatioCenter\times$ the center pure error standard deviation ($\sqrt{\text{MS}_{\text{PE, center}}} = \numSqrtMSPeCenterYone$). By contrast, the unweighted root-mean-square cell prediction error across the 25 unique design points is $\sqrt{\frac{1}{25}\sum_{i=1}^{25}(\bar{y}_i - \hat{y}_i)^2} \approx \numLofCellRmsUnweighted$, while the observation-weighted root-mean-square misfit across all 140 design evaluations is $\sqrt{\text{SS}_{\text{LoF}} / 140} \approx \numLofObsWeightedRms$ (down-weighting non-center cells relative to the replicated center).

To inspect where this lack of fit concentrates across the hypercube, per-design-point residual contributions $n_i (\bar{y}_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$ reveal that the single largest lack-of-fit discrepancy occurs at corner $(1, 1, -1, -1)$ ($x_1 = 1, x_2 = 1, x_3 = -1, x_4 = -1$, contribution $\approx \numLofCellContribMax$), where high learning rate and depth combined with low subsampling and regularization challenge second-order surface adequacy. Substantial discrepancies also concentrate at low learning rates ($x_1 = -1, \eta = 0.01$), notably at $(-1, -1, 1, 1)$ ($\numLofCellContribLowEtaOne$) and $(-1, 1, -1, 1)$ ($\numLofCellContribLowEtaTwo$), reflecting underfitting when 100 boosting iterations are paired with low step sizes. When refitting on the restricted sub-domain $x_1 \ge -0.5$ ($\eta \ge 0.033$), the sum of squares of lack of fit drops by $\numLofRestrictedReductionPct$ (from $\numSSLofYone$ to $\numSSLofRestricted$), and the RMS misfit declines by $\numLofRestrictedRmsDeclinePct$ to $\numSqrtMSLofRestricted$. However, we emphasize that dropping $x_1 = -1$ leaves only two factor levels ($x_1 \in \{0, 1\}$). Because two levels induce the identity $x_1^2 \equiv x_1$, separate linear and quadratic coefficients along Factor A are unidentifiable from those levels alone, reducing $\text{df}_{\text{LoF}}$ from 10 to 2. Consequently, this restricted test cannot assess quadratic curvature across $x_1 \in [0, 1]$ where all candidate optima reside. Even within this restricted region, lack of fit remains statistically significant ($F = \numFLofRestricted, p = 0.0001$), with RMS misfit ($\numSqrtMSLofRestricted$) remaining roughly $3\times$ the additive residual standard deviation ($\numSqrtMSPeRestricted$). This confirms that while low-$\eta$ underfitting drives the largest discrepancies, a second-order polynomial remains an approximation with non-negligible structural bias across gradient boosting loss surfaces.

For Latency ($Y_2$), structural lack of fit is non-significant against both reference baselines ($F = \numFLofCenterYtwo, p = \numPLofCenterYtwo$ against center pure error; $F = \numFLofYtwo, p = \numPLofYtwo$ against the saturated additive baseline). The treatment $\times$ block interaction is also non-significant ($F = \numFInteractCenterYtwo, p = \numPInteractCenterYtwo$), confirming that latency is invariant across seed blocks and data splits. To characterize the functional form of latency growth, five candidate models were compared against empirical measurements, as reported in Table \ref{tab:lat_models}. For the log-linear specification, AIC and BIC values are adjusted via the Jacobian of transformation ($+2 \sum \ln(y_i) = \numLatJacobian$) to allow direct likelihood comparison on the natural microsecond scale.

The quadratic latency model ($R^2 = \numLatQuadRsq$, adjusted $\text{AIC} = \numLatQuadAIC$) yields lower AIC than the linear model ($R^2 = \numLatLinRsq$, $\text{AIC} = \numLatLinAIC$) and the log-linear model (adjusted $\text{AIC} = \numLatLogAdjAIC$), consistent with the significant $x_2^2$ term in ANOVA ($F = \numAnovaLatencyFxTwoSq, p < 0.0001$). Latency exhibits super-linear growth across the empirical depth range ($d \in \{3, 6, 9\}$), with the quadratic fit capturing accelerating tree traversal costs while avoiding the severe over-prediction of exponential formulations. Comparing standard \texttt{predict} against \texttt{inplace\_predict} across the 140 historical DOE runs shows a mean interface overhead of $\numHistRunsOvMean \pm \numHistRunsOvSd\,\mu\text{s}$ (and $\numRevInterfaceOverhead \pm \numRevInterfaceOverheadSd\,\mu\text{s}$ in the 50-configuration Revision-v2 interface audit), indicating that \texttt{DMatrix} construction and wrapper validation add a consistent baseline latency offset while tree traversal scales super-linearly with depth.

\section{Statistical Residual Diagnostics}

To evaluate regression assumptions, diagnostic checks were conducted on the second-order Validation RMSE residuals, explicitly distinguishing grouping factors:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
    \item \textbf{Normality:} Evaluated via Shapiro-Wilk on the 140 second-order residuals: $W = \numShapiroW, p = \numShapiroP$, failing to reject the null hypothesis of Gaussian residuals at $\alpha = 0.05$.
    \item \textbf{Homoscedasticity Across Seed Blocks vs.\ Design Coordinates:} Mean-centered Levene's test across the \textbf{5 seed blocks} (\texttt{block} $1 \dots 5$) yields $W = \numLeveneW, p = \numLeveneP$, confirming uniform residual dispersion across data-split blocks. Median-centered Levene (Brown-Forsythe) testing across the \textbf{25 distinct design coordinates} yields $W = \numBrownForsytheW, p = \numBrownForsytheP$, because the 5 block observations within each coordinate share a common cell-mean offset ($\bar{y}_{i\cdot} - \hat{y}_i$) and exhibit similar within-coordinate spread around their cell median.
    \item \textbf{Reconciliation of Breusch-Pagan with Block and Coordinate Homogeneity:} The Breusch-Pagan test against continuous fitted values $\hat{y}$ is highly significant ($\text{LM} = \numBreuschPaganLM, p \numBreuschPaganP$). This occurs because Breusch-Pagan regresses squared OLS residuals $e_{ij}^2 = [(\bar{y}_{i\cdot} - \hat{y}_i) + (y_{ij} - \bar{y}_{i\cdot})]^2$ on the design regressors; since deterministic polynomial lack of fit $(\bar{y}_{i\cdot} - \hat{y}_i)^2$ is largest at the high-RMSE $\eta = 0.01$ boundary and compresses in the low-RMSE interior, squared residuals vary systematically across the factor space even though within-cell cross-block variance is homogeneous. This structural heteroscedasticity motivates reporting HC3 robust standard errors in Table \ref{tab:anova_ccd_rmse}, while recognizing that HC3 standard errors do not eliminate deterministic polynomial bias in prediction intervals.
    \item \textbf{Independence and Run Order:} Durbin-Watson statistic evaluated in actual randomized execution order yields $DW = \numDurbinWatson$. The Ljung-Box test ($Q = \numLjungBoxStat, p = \numLjungBoxP$) and Wald-Wolfowitz Runs test ($p = \numRunsTestP$) fail to detect serial correlation or thermal execution drift.
    \item \textbf{Influence and Leverage:} Maximum Cook's distance is $D_{\max} = \numMaxCooksD$, well below the commonly cited heuristic reference cutoff of $1.0$.
\end{enumerate}

Figure \ref{fig:diagnostics_panel} displays the 4-in-1 residual diagnostic panel.

\section{Phase 3: Canonical and Ridge Analysis}

\subsection{Matrix Representation and Stationary Point}

The fitted second-order model is expressed in matrix notation:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{y} = b_0 + \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{B} \mathbf{x}
\end{equation}
where $b_0 = \numBzero$ (averaging block effects equally), $\mathbf{b} = [\vecBOne, \vecBTwo, \vecBThree, \vecBFour]^T$, and:
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix}
        \matBOneOne & \matBOneTwo & \matBOneThree & \matBOneFour \\
        \matBTwoOne & \matBTwoTwo & \matBTwoThree & \matBTwoFour \\
        \matBThreeOne & \matBThreeTwo & \matBThreeThree & \matBThreeFour \\
        \matBFourOne & \matBFourTwo & \matBFourThree & \matBFourFour
    \end{bmatrix}
\end{equation}
The unconstrained stationary point $\mathbf{x}_0$ satisfies $\mathbf{b} + 2\mathbf{B}\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{0}$:
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{x}_0 = -\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{B}^{-1} \mathbf{b} = [\numStationaryXone, \numStationaryXtwo, \numStationaryXthree, \numStationaryXfour]^T
\end{equation}
The stationary coordinate along Factor C ($x_3 = \numStationaryXthree$) lies far outside the operational cube $[-1, +1]^4$. Its Euclidean distance from the coded origin is $\|\mathbf{x}_0\| = \numStationaryDistCoded$, while its Euclidean distance from the boundary of the feasible hypercube is $\numStationaryDistBoundary$ coded units. The unconstrained stationary point has a predicted response of $\hat{y}_0 = \numStationaryYhat$, an extrapolation artifact indicating that unconstrained quadratic optimization yields an infeasible point.

\subsection{Spectral Decomposition and Ridge Analysis}

Eigenvalues of $\mathbf{B}$ are $\lambda_1 = \numEigOne, \lambda_2 = \numEigTwo, \lambda_3 = \numEigThree, \lambda_4 = \numEigFour$ ($\sum \lambda_i = \text{trace}(\mathbf{B}) = \numTraceB$). While point estimates are positive, Rademacher wild bootstrap (2,000 replications) reveals that the 95\% bootstrap interval for $\lambda_1$ spans $[\numBootLowEigOne, \numBootHighEigOne]$, with $\numFracMinEigLeZero$ of bootstrap samples yielding $\min(\lambda) \le 0$. The canonical eigenvectors (columns of the orthogonal decomposition matrix $\mathbf{M}$) show that the smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ aligns along $\mathbf{v}_1 = [\eigVecOneOne, \allowbreak \eigVecOneTwo, \allowbreak \eigVecOneThree, \allowbreak \eigVecOneFour]^T$, representing a contrast between Factor C (subsampling, $\eigVecSignedOneThree$) and Factor D ($L_2$ regularization, $\eigVecSignedOneFour$), while $\lambda_2$ corresponds to $\mathbf{v}_2 = [\eigVecTwoOne, \allowbreak \eigVecTwoTwo, \allowbreak \eigVecTwoThree, \allowbreak \eigVecTwoFour]^T$, representing a joint direction along subsampling and regularization. By contrast, the dominant quadratic curvature axes align along Factor B (depth, $\mathbf{v}_3 = [\eigVecThreeOne, \allowbreak \eigVecThreeTwo, \allowbreak \eigVecThreeThree, \allowbreak \eigVecThreeFour]^T$, $\lambda_3 = \numEigThree$) and Factor A (learning rate, $\mathbf{v}_4 = [\eigVecFourOne, \allowbreak \eigVecFourTwo, \allowbreak \eigVecFourThree, \allowbreak \eigVecFourFour]^T$, $\lambda_4 = \numEigFour$). The system is classified as a \textbf{stationary or rising ridge}, with curvature along $x_3$ and $x_4$ statistically consistent with zero.

Constrained optimization over the hypercube $[-1, 1]^4$ with integer depth $d \in \{3, \dots, 9\}$ yields the results in Table \ref{tab:depth_opt}.

\section{Phase 4: Multi-Objective Desirability Optimization}

Minimizing predictive error requires deeper trees, which increases inference latency. To balance predictive error against inference latency, we use Derringer-Suich desirability functions \cite{derringer1980simultaneous}:
\begin{equation}
    d_r(Y_r) = \begin{cases}
        1.0, & Y_r < L_r \\
        \left(\frac{U_r - Y_r}{U_r - L_r}\right)^{s_r}, & L_r \le Y_r \le U_r \\
        0.0, & Y_r > U_r
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The composite desirability $D$ is formulated with explicit importance weights $(w_1, w_2)$:
\begin{equation}
    D = \left( d_1(Y_1)^{w_1} \cdot d_2(Y_2)^{w_2} \right)^{\frac{1}{w_1 + w_2}}
\end{equation}
In the baseline scenario, equal weights $w_1 = 1, w_2 = 1$ are used with engineering limits $L_1 = 0.450, U_1 = 0.700$ for RMSE and $L_2 = 100.0, U_2 = 180.0\ \mu\text{s}$ for latency ($s_1 = s_2 = 1.0$). 

To select a deployable operating point, desirability $D$ was evaluated across a high-resolution factor grid ($21 \times 7 \times 2 \times 2 = 588$ design coordinates) with discrete depths $d \in \{3, \dots, 9\}$. While unconstrained maximization pushes toward the upper boundary $\eta \to 0.30$ ($x_1 = 1.0$, reaching $D = \numDesirabilityBoundaryMax$) due to the 100-tree ceiling, operating directly on boundary edges risks boundary extrapolation. Holding depth $d=\numOptDepth$, subsample $1.0$, and $\lambda = \numOptLambdaThreeDp$, composite desirability varies smoothly across the interior: $D = \numDesirabilityEtaPointTwoZero$ at $\eta = 0.20$, $D = \numOptD$ at $\eta = \numOptEta$, $D = \numDesirabilityEtaPointTwoFive$ at $\eta = 0.25$, and $D = \numDesirabilityEtaPointThreeZero$ at $\eta = 0.30$. We chose the interior coordinate at $x_1 = \numOptXone$ ($\eta = \numOptEta$) as the selected operational multi-objective compromise configuration $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$:
\begin{align}
    \mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}} &= [\numOptXone, \numOptXtwo, \numOptXthree, \numOptXfour]^T \nonumber \\
    &\implies (\eta = \numOptEta, \text{depth} = \numOptDepth, \text{subsample} = \numOptSubsample, \lambda = \numOptLambda)
\end{align}
achieving $D = \numOptD$ ($d_1 = \numOptdOne, d_2 = \numOptdTwo$). Predicted metrics at $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ are $\hat{Y}_1 = \numPredRMSE$ and $\hat{Y}_2 = \numPredLatency\ \mu\text{s}$. 

Table \ref{tab:desirability_sensitivity} reports sensitivity across alternative specification limits and weights. Across all scenarios, the optimal depth clusters between 3 and 5, indicating that shallow-to-moderate tree depths provide the best balance between accuracy and latency.

\section{Phase 5: Empirical Confirmation and Benchmark Comparison}

\subsection{Confirmation Experiments at Multi-Objective and Single-Objective Optima}
\label{sec:confirmation}

To test surrogate fidelity, $m = 10$ confirmation trials were executed at $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ across fresh seeds disjoint from the design ($\mathcal{S}_{\text{conf}} = \{505, 606, 707, 808, 909, 1010, 1111, 1212, 1313, 1414\}$). Because fresh seeds introduce block variance ($\sigma^2_{\text{block}}$ estimated with only $4$~df) alongside model parameter covariance ($\text{MS}_E$ with $121$~df), treating block variance uncertainty as negligible would understate interval width. The total theoretical variance for the confirmation mean $\bar{y}_m$ at coordinate $\mathbf{x}_0$ with leverage $h_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^T (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_0$ is:
\begin{equation}
    V_{\text{conf}} = \sigma^2_E \left(\frac{1}{m} + h_0\right) + \sigma^2_{\text{block}}\left(\frac{1}{m} + \frac{1}{5}\right)
\end{equation}
Under the randomized block design with $a = 28$ runs per block, the expected mean squares satisfy $\mathbb{E}[\text{MS}_E] = \sigma^2_E$ and $\mathbb{E}[\text{MS}_{\text{block}}] = \sigma^2_E + 28\,\sigma^2_{\text{block}}$, giving the unbiased ANOVA estimator $\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{block}} = (\text{MS}_{\text{block}} - \text{MS}_E)/28$. Substituting $\hat{\sigma}^2_{\text{block}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}^2_E = \text{MS}_E$ into $V_{\text{conf}}$ yields the linear combination of independent mean squares required by Satterthwaite's synthesis:
\begin{equation}
    \hat{V}_{\text{conf}} = \text{MS}_E \left(\frac{1}{m} + h_0\right) + \frac{\text{MS}_{\text{block}} - \text{MS}_E}{28}\left(\frac{1}{m} + \frac{1}{5}\right) = c_1 \text{MS}_E + c_2 \text{MS}_{\text{block}}
\end{equation}
where $c_2 = \frac{1/m + 1/5}{28}$ and $c_1 = (1/m + h_0) - c_2$. Propagating variance-component degrees of freedom via Satterthwaite's approximation yields effective degrees of freedom:
\begin{equation}
    \nu_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\hat{V}_{\text{conf}}^2}{\frac{(c_1 \text{MS}_E)^2}{121} + \frac{(c_2 \text{MS}_{\text{block}})^2}{4}}
\end{equation}
For $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ ($h_0 = \numConfLeverageH$), Satterthwaite effective degrees of freedom evaluate to $\nu_{\text{eff}} = \numConfNuEffMo$ ($t_{0.025, \numConfNuEffMo} = \numConfTCritMo$), widening the 95\% prediction interval to $[\numConfPiLowValRMSE, \numConfPiHighValRMSE]$ (compared to $[\numConfNaivePiLowValRMSE, \numConfNaivePiHighValRMSE]$ under the unadjusted $t_{0.025, 121}$ approximation). For the depth-7 single-objective coordinate $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ ($h_0 = \numConfSoLeverageH$), $\nu_{\text{eff}} = \numConfSoNuEffSo$ ($t_{0.025, \numConfSoNuEffSo} = \numConfSoTCrit$), producing $[\numConfSoPiLowValRMSE, \numConfSoPiHighValRMSE]$. We note that Satterthwaite prediction intervals pool structural lack of fit (10~df) and treatment $\times$ block interaction (96~df) into $\text{MS}_E$, assuming homogeneous residual variance across design cells without safeguarding against local polynomial bias. Table \ref{tab:confirmation} compares predictions against empirical results.

For the multi-objective compromise coordinate $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ (depth 4), empirical validation RMSE of $\numConfEmpValRMSE \pm \numConfEmpValRMSEStd$ falls directly inside the Satterthwaite prediction interval ($[\numConfPiLowValRMSE, \numConfPiHighValRMSE]$), providing pointwise confirmation consistent with the surrogate. Empirical latency was $\numConfEmpLat \pm \numConfEmpLatStd\,\mu\text{s}$, also falling within $[\numConfPiLowLatOneDp, \numConfPiHighLatOneDp]\,\mu\text{s}$. Test RMSE on the external holdout set ($N = 4{,}128$) averaged $\numConfEmpTestRMSE \pm \numConfEmpTestRMSEStd$. Pointwise confirmation at $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ does not imply global surrogate accuracy across the entire hypercube.

For the single-objective candidate $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ (depth 7), the surrogate predicted $\hat{y} = \numConfSoPredValRMSE$ with Satterthwaite 95\% PI $[\numConfSoPiLowValRMSE, \numConfSoPiHighValRMSE]$, while empirical confirmation yielded $\numConfSoEmpValRMSE \pm \numConfSoEmpValRMSEStd$. Because empirical validation RMSE lies $\numConfSoExceedance$ above the upper bound of the Satterthwaite interval, the prediction was not confirmed. The surrogate exhibited structural optimism of $\numConfSoBias$ ($\numConfSoBiasSeMult\times \text{SE}(\hat{y})$), indicating that quadratic interpolation between sampled design depths $\{3, 6, 9\}$ does not adequately track the diminishing returns of deeper trees. Measured inference latency ($\numConfSoEmpLat \pm \numConfSoEmpLatStd\,\mu\text{s}$) sits directly on the lower prediction interval bound ($\numConfSoPiLowLatOneDp\,\mu\text{s}$), representing a borderline confirmation. On the holdout test set, depth 7 achieves an external test RMSE of $\numConfSoEmpTestRMSE \pm \numConfSoEmpTestRMSEStd$, competitive with Bayesian baselines.

\subsection{Provenance of Numerical Similarities Across Confirmation and Benchmark Evaluations}

Several summary metrics across Table \ref{tab:confirmation} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks} match or nearly match to four decimal places ($\numConfEmpValRMSE$, $\numConfSoEmpValRMSE$, $\numHistBenchSoValRMSEFourDp$, $\numConfSoEmpTestRMSE$, $\numConfEmpTestRMSE$) for distinct structural or statistical reasons:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.8em, itemsep=0.25em]
    \item \textbf{Shared Configuration Hash and Shared 20-Seed Evaluation Pool (\texttt{doe-so-historical}, \texttt{doe-mo-historical}, and \texttt{doe-so-rep-0..19}):} Both the historical benchmark script (\texttt{scripts/run\_benchmarks.py}) and the Revision-v2 evaluator (\texttt{final\_evaluation.py}) evaluate frozen configurations across the exact same 20 fresh seeds $\mathcal{S}_{\text{eval}} = \{2001, \dots, 2020\}$ on the 75/25 split of the 16,512-row development pool and the 4,128-row external holdout test set. Consequently, \texttt{doe-so-historical} (\texttt{config\_sha256 = 0079fbae0ec5b7cb\dots}: $\eta = \numCubeOptEta, d = \numCubeOptDepth, s = \numCubeOptSubsample, \lambda = \numCubeOptLambda$) and \texttt{doe-mo-historical} (\texttt{config\_sha256 = b05e8e5cb67e8668\dots}: $\eta = \numOptEta, d = \numOptDepth, s = \numOptSubsample, \lambda = \numOptLambda$) yield identical full-precision RMSEs across \texttt{results/benchmark.csv} and \texttt{final\_evaluations.csv} ($\text{Test RMSE} = \numHistBenchSoTestRMSEFull$, $\text{Val RMSE} = \numHistBenchSoValRMSEFull$ for \texttt{doe-so-historical}; $\text{Test RMSE} = \numHistBenchMoTestRMSEFull$, $\text{Val RMSE} = \numHistBenchMoValRMSEFull$ for \texttt{doe-mo-historical}) while differing in latency due to separate timing sessions. Meanwhile, in Revision-v2, all 20 Repeated DOE Single-Objective replicates select the exact same boundary grid point (\texttt{grid\_index = \numRevDoeSoRepGridIdx}, \texttt{config\_sha256 = 9d7c4e74ff156870\dots}: $\eta = \numRevDoeSoRepEta, d = \numCubeOptDepth, s = \numCubeOptSubsample, \lambda = \numCubeOptLambda$) on the predeclared \numRevDoeGridSize-point grid. Because \texttt{final\_evaluation.py} deduplicates model training by \texttt{config\_sha256} across seeds $2001\dots2020$, all 20 \texttt{doe-so-rep-r} records map to the exact same 20 trained XGBoost boosters, yielding identical means ($\text{Test RMSE} = \numRevDoeSoTestRMSEFull$, $\text{Val RMSE} = \numRevDoeSoValRMSEFull$, rounding to $\numRevDoeSoTestRMSEFourDp$ and $\numRevDoeSoValRMSEFourDp$) and zero between-search variance ($\text{SD} = \numRevDoeSoTestRMSESd$).
    \item \textbf{Disjoint Seed Sets Agreeing at Four Decimal Places ($\mathcal{S}_{\text{conf}} = \{505, \dots, 1414\}$ vs.\ $\mathcal{S}_{\text{eval}} = \{2001, \dots, 2020\}$):} Phase~5 confirmation evaluates $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ and $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ across $m=10$ seeds completely disjoint from $\mathcal{S}_{\text{eval}}$. At $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ ($d=4$), the 10-seed confirmation validation RMSE mean is $\numConfMoValRMSEFull$ ($\text{SD} = \numConfEmpValRMSEStd$), whereas the 20-replicate Repeated DOE MO validation RMSE mean across seeds $2001\dots2020$ is $\numRevDoeMoValRMSEFull$ ($\text{SD} = \numRevDoeMoValRMSESd$); both round to $\numConfEmpValRMSE$ at four decimal places despite using disjoint seed sets and distinct candidate coordinates (10-seed confirmation holdout test RMSE is $\numConfMoTestRMSEFull \pm \numConfMoTestRMSESdFull$, rounding to $\numConfEmpTestRMSE$, vs.\ $\numHistBenchMoTestRMSEFull \pm \numHistBenchMoTestRMSESdFull$, rounding to $\numHistBenchMoTestRMSEFourDp$, on the 20 benchmark seeds and $\numRevDoeMoTestRMSE$ or $\numRevDoeMoTestRMSEFourDp$ at 4 decimal places for Repeated DOE MO). Likewise, at $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ ($d=7$), the 10-seed confirmation validation RMSE mean is $\numConfSoValRMSEFull$ ($\text{SD} = \numConfSoEmpValRMSEStd$) and the 20-replicate Constrained TPE validation RMSE mean on seeds $2001\dots2020$ is $\numRevCtpeValRMSEFull$, both rounding to $\numConfSoEmpValRMSE$ at four decimal places; on the holdout test set, the 10-seed confirmation mean at $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ is $\numConfSoTestRMSEFull$ ($\text{SD} = \numConfSoTestRMSESdFull$, rounding to $\numConfSoEmpTestRMSE$) versus $\numHistBenchSoTestRMSEFull$ ($\text{SD} = \numHistBenchSoTestRMSESdFull$, rounding to $\numDoeSoTestRMSE$, differing by $\numDiffConfBenchSoTestRMSE$ RMSE) on the 20 benchmark seeds.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Benchmark Evaluation Against Random Search and Optuna TPE}

To compare the pre-planned Design of Experiments framework against modern heuristic and Bayesian search algorithms under equal evaluation budgets (140 function evaluations per search), we executed a prospective benchmark campaign across $N = 20$ independent search replicates per optimizer:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Unguided Random Search:} 20 independent replicates of 140 evaluations uniformly sampled across the 4-factor domain.
    \item \textbf{Single-Objective TPE:} 20 independent replicates of 140 evaluations optimizing validation RMSE via Tree-structured Parzen Estimators \cite{bergstra2011algorithms, akiba2019optuna}.
    \item \textbf{Constrained TPE:} Single-objective TPE with an operational inference latency constraint ($\le 145\,\mu\text{s}$) evaluated via single-threaded single-sample prediction latency measured online during trial sampling (30 calls without warmup).
    \item \textbf{Multi-Objective TPE:} Evaluates validation RMSE and online 30-call single-sample prediction latency simultaneously to construct a candidate Pareto front, followed by post-hoc operating coordinate selection via Derringer-Suich desirability.
    \item \textbf{Repeated Pre-Planned DOE Formulations:} 20 independent replicates of the pre-planned 140-run Face-Centered Central Composite Design across fresh 5-block seed quintuplets (seeds $3001$--$3100$), evaluating both the multi-objective compromise $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ (depth 4) and the single-objective candidate $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ (depth 7).
\end{enumerate}

Across the six methods, winning hyperparameter configurations from the 20 search replicates (\numRevTotalSelectionRecords\ selection records representing \numRevTotalDistinctConfigs\ distinct configuration hashes, yielding \numRevTotalEvaluationRows\ final evaluation rows) were serialized into an immutable manifest (\texttt{finalized\_selections.json}, verified by SHA-256) prior to holdout evaluation. Across the prospective benchmark campaign, \numRevTotalFits\ XGBoost model fits and \numRevTotalTimedInferences\ timed prediction evaluations (\numRevTotalAllInferences\ total prediction calls including \numRevTotalWarmupInferences\ untimed warmup calls) were executed.

Crucially, we clarify the history of the holdout test set: the historical v1.0.0 experiments recorded test results during development, whereas the revised Revision-v2 pipeline programmatically prevented access to those test labels during all search iterations, surrogate fitting, and desirability calculations until winning configurations were frozen in \texttt{finalized\_selections.json}. While these safeguards enforce pipeline isolation during the revised experiments, they cannot undo earlier historical exposure of the same dataset. Each frozen hyperparameter configuration was then retrained from scratch and evaluated across 20 fresh seeds (seeds $2001$--$2020$, $\mathcal{S}_{\text{eval}}$) on the external holdout test set under dedicated single-threaded latency profiling ($2\times 500$ timed single-row calls per seed with $50$ warmup calls per session, pinned to CPU Core~0). Because both historical v1.0.0 scripts (\texttt{scripts/run\_confirmation.py} and \texttt{scripts/run\_benchmarks.py}) also applied Win32 CPU core~0 affinity pinning, the latency difference between historical single-run snapshots and the prospective campaign reflects between-session system timing drift ($\text{SD} = \numRevBetweenSessionSd\,\mu\text{s}$ across repeated sessions) rather than unpinned execution.

The prospective empirical benchmarks establish six key scientific findings:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.8em, itemsep=0.3em, topsep=0.3em]
    \item \textbf{Single-Objective Predictive Performance vs.\ Latency:} Single-Objective TPE achieves the numerically lowest observed mean Test RMSE ($\numRevSoTpeTestRMSE \pm \numRevSoTpeTestRMSESd$), selecting deep trees ($d \in \{7, 8, 9\}$) with an average inference latency of $\numRevSoTpePredictLat \pm \numRevSoTpePredictLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$ (inplace $\numRevSoTpeInplaceLat\,\mu\text{s}$). Neither Single-Objective TPE nor Repeated DOE Single-Objective satisfies the $\le 145\,\mu\text{s}$ latency constraint ($0/20$ feasible). Repeated DOE Single-Objective ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$, depth~7) achieves a mean Test RMSE of $\numRevDoeSoTestRMSE$ at $\numRevDoeSoPredictLat \pm \numRevDoeSoPredictLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$ latency ($\numRevDoeSoLatLowerPct$ lower latency than SO-TPE).
    \item \textbf{What Repeated DOE Replicates Represent and Separation of Selection vs.\ Retraining Variance:} Each of the $N=20$ Repeated DOE replicates ($r \in \{0, \dots, 19\}$) executes a fresh 140-run blocked FCCD across 5 disjoint block seeds ($3001 + 5r$ to $3005 + 5r$, spanning seeds $3001\dots3100$) drawn from the 16,512-row development pool, fits OLS second-order surfaces for validation RMSE and latency, and selects candidates over a deterministic \numRevDoeGridSize-point predeclared grid (\texttt{doe\_selection\_protocol.json}: $21$ coded learning-rate levels $x_1 \in [-1, +1] \times 7$ integer depths $d \in \{3, \dots, 9\} \times 3$ coded subsample levels $x_3 \in \{-1, 0, +1\} \times 3$ coded regularization levels $x_4 \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$). Because the single-objective minimum on this grid consistently lies at the same boundary coordinate (\texttt{grid\_index = \numRevDoeSoRepGridIdx}, $x = [+0.6, +1/3, +1.0, +1.0]^T \implies \eta = \numRevDoeSoRepEta, d = 7, s = 1.0, \lambda = \numCubeOptLambda$), all 20 DOE-SO replicates select the identical configuration hash (\texttt{9d7c4e74ff156870\dots}), yielding between-search selection $\text{SD} = \numRevDoeSoTestRMSESd$; its non-zero uncertainty is captured entirely by the conditional retraining standard deviation $\sigma_{\text{eval}} = \numRevDoeSoRetrainSd$ across the 20 evaluation seeds $2001\dots2020$. For DOE-MO, desirability optimization over feasible grid points selects across \numRevDoeMoRepUniqueConfigs\ distinct grid configurations in $d \in \{4, 5\}$, yielding between-search $\text{SD} = \numRevDoeMoTestRMSESd$ alongside conditional retraining $\sigma_{\text{eval}} = \numRevDoeMoRetrainSd$.
    \item \textbf{Multi-Objective Statistical Comparison (Primary Unpaired Welch vs.\ Secondary Index-Paired Test):} Comparing multi-objective solutions, Repeated DOE ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$, depth~4) achieves a mean Test RMSE of $\numRevDoeMoTestRMSE \pm \numRevDoeMoTestRMSESd$ at $\numRevDoeMoPredictLat \pm \numRevDoeMoPredictLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$ latency (inplace $\numRevDoeMoInplaceLat\,\mu\text{s}$), closely matching Multi-Objective TPE which achieves $\numRevMoTpeTestRMSE \pm \numRevMoTpeTestRMSESd$ at $\numRevMoTpePredictLat \pm \numRevMoTpePredictLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$ (inplace $\numRevMoTpeInplaceLat\,\mu\text{s}$). Because replicate index $r \in \{0, \dots, 19\}$ pairs DOE block seeds $3001+5r\dots3005+5r$ with Optuna sampler seed $1000+r$ on split~42 rather than a shared random block, Welch's two-sample $t$-test is the primary inferential comparison ($\Delta = \numRevDiffDoeMoMoTpe$ RMSE, $t = \numRevWelchTDoeMoMoTpe, p = \numRevWelchPDoeMoMoTpe$), while the replicate-index paired $t$-test ($t = \numRevPairedTDoeMoMoTpe, p = \numRevPairedPDoeMoMoTpe$) is reported as a secondary sensitivity check. Because no pre-registered equivalence margin was specified, this non-significant difference indicates no detected performance gap rather than formal statistical equivalence. Both multi-objective methods achieve $100\%$ benchmark constraint feasibility ($20/20$).
    \item \textbf{Development Hypervolume vs.\ Holdout Non-Dominated Set and Seed-Bootstrap Uncertainty:} On development split~42 under 30-call search timing, MO-TPE candidate fronts attain a mean hypervolume of $\numRevHvMoTpeDevMean \pm \numRevHvMoTpeDevSd$ at reference $[0.60, 250.0]$ ($\numRevHvMoTpeDevMeanRefTwo \pm \numRevHvMoTpeDevSdRefTwo$ at $[0.65, 275.0]$), exceeding the fixed 27-point DOE candidate frontier ($\numRevHvFullDoeDev$, 1-sample difference $\numRevHvDiffDev, p < 0.0001$; at $[0.65, 275.0]$, $\numRevHvFullDoeDevRefTwo$, difference $\numRevHvDiffDevRefTwo, p < 0.0001$), while Repeated DOE 5-block means achieve $\numRevHvDoeDevMean \pm \numRevHvDoeDevSd$. On the external holdout test set across 20 retraining seeds, \numRevHoldoutNonDominatedConfigs\ distinct configurations form the empirical non-dominated set among the \numRevTotalSelectionRecords\ frozen selections (hypervolume $\numRevHvHoldoutFrozen$ at $[0.60, 250.0]$ and $\numRevHvHoldoutFrozenRefTwo$ at $[0.65, 275.0]$): 3 Repeated DOE MO, 3 MO-TPE, 5 Constrained TPE, and 1 SO-TPE. Paired cluster bootstrap resampling ($B = 2{,}000$ resamples over the 20 shared evaluation seeds $2001\dots2020$) yields a holdout frontier hypervolume of $\numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedMean \pm \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedSd$ (95\% CI $[\numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedCiLow, \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedCiHigh]$) at $[0.60, 250.0]$ and $\numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedMeanRefTwo \pm \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedSdRefTwo$ (95\% CI $[\numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedCiLowRefTwo, \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedCiHighRefTwo]$) at $[0.65, 275.0]$ (joint seed-plus-session bootstrap: $\numRevHvHoldoutBootJointMean \pm \numRevHvHoldoutBootJointSd$, 95\% CI $[\numRevHvHoldoutBootJointCiLow, \numRevHvHoldoutBootJointCiHigh]$). Across the $2{,}000$ seed-bootstrap frontiers, Repeated DOE MO, MO-TPE, and Constrained TPE each contribute at least one non-dominated configuration in $\numRevBootPresentPctDoeMo$, $\numRevBootPresentPctMoTpe$, and $\numRevBootPresentPctCTpe$ of resamples (mean frontier points: $\numRevBootMeanPtsDoeMo$, $\numRevBootMeanPtsMoTpe$, and $\numRevBootMeanPtsCTpe$), while SO-TPE contributes in $\numRevBootPresentPctSoTpe$ (mean $\numRevBootMeanPtsSoTpe$ points).
    \item \textbf{Constrained TPE Feasibility Dynamics:} Constrained TPE achieves $\numRevCtpeSearchFeas$ feasibility during search under online 30-call timing, but yields $\numRevCtpeBenchFeas$ ($\numRevCtpeBenchFeasPct$) feasibility under the 1,000-call benchmark evaluation protocol ($\numRevCtpeDepthSixLat \pm \numRevCtpeDepthSixLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$ for depth~6 selections, $9/9$ feasible; $\numRevCtpeDepthSevenLat \pm \numRevCtpeDepthSevenLatSd\,\mu\text{s}$ for depth~7 selections, $0/11$ feasible). Plausible explanations include noisy 30-call search measurements near the boundary, protocol differences (30 calls without warmup vs.\ 1,000 calls with warmup), and winner's-curse selection bias near the $145\,\mu\text{s}$ threshold.
    \item \textbf{Computational Budget Reconciliation and Wall-Clock Cost:} Table \ref{tab:computational_budget} reconciles all model fits, distinct coordinates, timed inferences, untimed warmup calls, and per-replicate search wall-clock times across both campaigns. Although each search replicate executes exactly 140 XGBoost fits, mean training time per fit and wall-clock time per replicate vary systematically with the depth and learning-rate distribution sampled by each algorithm: Repeated Blocked DOE averages $\numRevWallTimeDoeMean \pm \numRevWallTimeDoeSd\,\text{s}$ per replicate ($\numRevFitMsDoe\,\text{ms/fit}$, shared across DOE-MO and DOE-SO), Multi-Objective TPE averages $\numRevWallTimeMoTpeMean \pm \numRevWallTimeMoTpeSd\,\text{s}$ ($\numRevFitMsMoTpe\,\text{ms/fit}$), Constrained TPE averages $\numRevWallTimeCTpeMean \pm \numRevWallTimeCTpeSd\,\text{s}$ ($\numRevFitMsCTpe\,\text{ms/fit}$), Random Search averages $\numRevWallTimeRsMean \pm \numRevWallTimeRsSd\,\text{s}$ ($\numRevFitMsRs\,\text{ms/fit}$), and Single-Objective TPE requires $\numRevWallTimeSoTpeMean \pm \numRevWallTimeSoTpeSd\,\text{s}$ ($\numRevFitMsSoTpe\,\text{ms/fit}$) because adaptive concentration in depths $7$--$9$ increases tree construction cost.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion and Limitations}

The empirical findings clarify the trade-offs between classical Design of Experiments and adaptive Bayesian optimization:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=1.8em]
    \item \textbf{Parametric Attribution and Variance Decomposition vs.\ Adaptive Coordinate Exploration:} Pre-planned blocked DOE provides orthogonal main-effect and interaction attribution, formal non-planarity testing ($F = \numFCurv$ against center pure error; $F = \numCurvFBlockPaired$ across the 5 seed blocks), multi-scale lack-of-fit diagnostics ($F = \numFLofYone$), and high selection stability across replicates (between-search $\text{SD} = \numRevDoeSoTestRMSESd$ for DOE-SO and $\numRevDoeMoTestRMSESd$ for DOE-MO). However, spending 140 runs to replicate 25 fixed coordinates across 5 blocks limits spatial coverage and allocates $\numDoeLowEtaCount/140$ runs ($\numDoeLowEtaPct$) to the severe underfitting boundary ($\eta = 0.01$). Conversely, adaptive TPE explores 140 distinct coordinates and concentrates trials near promising interior regions, achieving lower single-objective Test RMSE ($\numRevSoTpeTestRMSE$ vs.\ $\numRevDoeSoTestRMSE$) and higher single-split development candidate hypervolume ($\numRevHvMoTpeDevMean$ vs.\ $\numRevHvFullDoeDev$), at the expense of higher selection variance and no parametric decomposition.
    \item \textbf{Stochastic Seed Blocking:} Random complete block design isolated an estimated $\sigma_{\text{block}} \approx \numSigmaBlock$ RMSE in unexplained residual variance ($\text{ICC} = \numICCAnova$, or $\numICCAnovaPct$; REML $\text{ICC} = \numICCReml$). While primary factors account for $>90\%$ of total sum of squares across the wide hypercube, this seed-to-seed partition shift exceeds the differences separating competitive configurations near the optimum, demonstrating the importance of blocking when comparing configurations across data splits.
    \item \textbf{Structural Lack of Fit and Surrogate Optimism:} Second-order polynomials cannot globally match the asymmetric saturation of gradient boosting loss across an order-of-magnitude learning-rate range. This structural limitation produced significant lack of fit ($F = \numFLofYone, p = \numPLofYone$, $\sqrt{\text{MS}_{\text{LoF}}} = \numSqrtMSLofYone$) and surrogate optimism at intermediate depth~7 ($\text{bias} = \numConfSoBias$, $\numConfSoBiasSeMult\times \text{SE}(\hat{y})$). Because Satterthwaite prediction intervals pool structural lack of fit (10~df) and treatment $\times$ block interaction (96~df) into $\text{MS}_E$, they widen intervals under unexplained variance but do not protect against localized deterministic polynomial bias.
    \item \textbf{Latency Protocol Sensitivity and Interface Overhead:} Single-sample inference latency follows super-linear growth across discrete depths ($R^2 = \numLatQuadRsq$), while standard \texttt{predict} incurs a consistent wrapper and \texttt{DMatrix} construction overhead of $\numRevInterfaceOverhead \pm \numRevInterfaceOverheadSd\,\mu\text{s}$ ($\numHistRunsOvMean \pm \numHistRunsOvSd\,\mu\text{s}$ in historical runs) over \texttt{inplace\_predict}. Furthermore, Constrained TPE's drop from $\numRevCtpeSearchFeas$ search feasibility (30 un-warmed calls) to $\numRevCtpeBenchFeas$ benchmark feasibility (1,000 warmed calls) demonstrates that online latency constraints require warmed multi-call verification and safety margins near operational thresholds.
    \item \textbf{Scope and Dimensionality Scaling:} These conclusions apply to XGBoost with 100 boosting trees on the California Housing dataset across $k=4$ hyperparameters. Because full factorial and central composite designs scale as $2^k + 2k + n_c$ per block, pre-planned second-order designs become prohibitive in higher dimensions ($k > 8$) without fractional factorial screening (Resolution IV/V) or hybrid screening-plus-Bayesian refinement.
\end{enumerate}

The repository preserves three auditable provenance milestones by immutable Git commit SHA: (i) the historical v1.0.0 baseline at commit \texttt{c6deac1f2d9eb7fb4a20\allowbreak 7fd97a63e5eeb0b5df1e} (140 blocked FCCD runs, 20 confirmation runs, and single-run Split-42 benchmarks); (ii) the prospective Revision-v2 experimental campaign at commit \texttt{97d882e982909874c527\allowbreak a158c3c27bf1c1fa9da2} (\numRevTotalFits\ model fits and \numRevTotalTimedInferences\ timed inferences in \texttt{results/revision\_v2/\allowbreak full\_run\_001/}); and (iii) the Work Package D.2 single-source-of-truth reporting and SHA-256 evidence-lock architecture at commit \texttt{6b53dac85af261553a78\allowbreak 70f4888d5ea7423d4b5e}. All experimental designs, XGBoost model executions, and raw CSV/JSON artifacts were produced by deterministic Python scripts executed locally on the target hardware; no experimental metrics were synthesized or estimated by language models. Every numerical claim in this manuscript and its companion report is programmatically generated and verified against the 40 SHA-256-locked evidence files via \texttt{scripts/\allowbreak reporting\_data.py}, \texttt{scripts/\allowbreak generate\_report\_artifacts.py}, \texttt{scripts/\allowbreak generate\_research\_reporting.py}, and continuous integration checks on Ubuntu and Windows.

\section{Conclusion}

This study evaluated a pre-planned blocked Design of Experiments (DOE) and Response Surface Methodology (RSM) framework for multi-objective hyperparameter optimization in gradient boosted decision trees. Using a randomized complete block design across 5 data-split blocks ($N=140$ runs across 25 FCCD coordinates), the framework isolated stochastic partition variance ($\sigma_{\text{block}} \approx \numSigmaBlock$, $\text{ICC} = \numICCAnova$), confirmed strong non-planarity across six error denominators ($F = \numFCurv$ against center pure error; $F = \numCurvFBlockPaired$ across blocks), and identified an interior multi-objective compromise configuration ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$, depth~4) via Derringer-Suich desirability. Empirical confirmation across $m=10$ fresh seeds validated the Satterthwaite prediction intervals at $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$ ($\numConfEmpValRMSE \pm \numConfEmpValRMSEStd$ validation RMSE; $\numConfEmpLat \pm \numConfEmpLatStd\,\mu\text{s}$ latency), while exposing structural polynomial optimism at the single-objective candidate $\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{SO}}$ ($\numConfSoBias$ RMSE bias at depth~7).

Prospective benchmark evaluations comprising \numRevTotalFits\ model fits across 20 independent search replicates and 20 fresh retraining seeds on an external holdout test set demonstrated the complementary strengths of pre-planned DOE and adaptive Bayesian optimization. Single-Objective TPE achieved the lowest mean holdout Test RMSE ($\numRevSoTpeTestRMSE \pm \numRevSoTpeTestRMSESd$) at higher latency ($\numRevSoTpePredictLat\,\mu\text{s}$) and longer search wall-clock time ($\numRevWallTimeSoTpeMean\,\text{s}$), whereas Repeated DOE Single-Objective achieved deterministic grid selection ($\numRevDoeSoTestRMSE$, between-search $\text{SD} = \numRevDoeSoTestRMSESd$, retraining $\sigma_{\text{eval}} = \numRevDoeSoRetrainSd$) with $\numRevDoeSoLatLowerPct$ lower latency ($\numRevDoeSoPredictLat\,\mu\text{s}$). In the latency-constrained multi-objective regime ($\le 145\,\mu\text{s}$), Repeated DOE ($\mathbf{x}^*_{\text{MO}}$) and Multi-Objective TPE achieved 100\% benchmark feasibility ($20/20$) with no statistically significant difference in holdout Test RMSE ($\numRevDoeMoTestRMSE$ vs.\ $\numRevMoTpeTestRMSE$, Welch $p = \numRevWelchPDoeMoMoTpeTwoDp$) at comparable single-sample latency ($\numRevDoeMoPredictLatOneDp\,\mu\text{s}$ vs.\ $\numRevMoTpePredictLatOneDp\,\mu\text{s}$). While MO-TPE achieved higher development candidate hypervolume on split~42 ($\numRevHvMoTpeDevMean$ vs.\ $\numRevHvFullDoeDev$ for the 27-point DOE front), holdout evaluation across 20 retraining seeds yielded a \numRevHoldoutNonDominatedConfigs-configuration empirical non-dominated set ($\text{HV} = \numRevHvHoldoutFrozen$, seed-bootstrap 95\% CI $[\numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedCiLow, \numRevHvHoldoutBootSeedCiHigh]$) populated jointly by DOE and TPE selections. Classical blocked DOE and RSM thus provide a transparent, variance-shielded complement to adaptive Bayesian search for latency-constrained tabular machine learning.
